quote: Beweise den Satz: Eine quinäre quadratische Diophantische Gl. ist in dem durch ihre Coefficienten be- stimmten Rationalitätsbe- reiche stets lösbar, wenn sie in dem bez. reellen Körper nicht definit ist.
english: Prove the theorem: a quinary quadratic Diophantine equation is always solvable in the domain of rationality determined by its coefficients if it is not definite in the corresponding real field.
topic: A pasted-in plan for Hilbert's future number-theoretic studies (relative abelian fields, Fermat's theorem, complex multiplication), followed by notes on solvability of quadratic and higher-degree Diophantine equations, a remark on Molien's paper on hypercomplex numbers, and an elementary proof of the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality after Hurwitz.

triage.modern_statement: Take a number field K, meaning the field generated by the coefficients, and a nondegenerate quadratic form Q(x1,...,x5) over K. Suppose Q is indefinite at every real embedding of K. Then Q(x)=0 has a nontrivial solution in K^5, i.e. Q is isotropic over K. Over K=Q this is Meyer's theorem. For a general number field it follows from the Hasse–Minkowski local-global principle together with the fact that every quadratic form in at least 5 variables over a p-adic field is isotropic.
triage.answered_by: A. Meyer (1884) proved the case of rational coefficients. Hilbert's own notebook note goes further, to forms whose coefficients lie in an algebraic number field, and that general case follows from Hasse's 1923–24 local-global principle for quadratic forms over number fields (the Hasse–Minkowski theorem). This is the setting of Hilbert's 11th Problem from 1900, which asks about quadratic forms with algebraic coefficients.

evidence.claim: Meyer's theorem: an indefinite quadratic form in five or more variables over Q has a nontrivial rational zero.
Hasse proved the Hasse principle for quadratic forms over an arbitrary number field k in 1923–1924.
In 1924 Hasse extended Minkowski's result to arbitrary number fields (Hasse–Minkowski theorem).
Hilbert's 11th problem (1900) asks for the theory of quadratic forms in any number of variables with algebraic coefficients, including solving quadratic equations with algebraic coefficients.
The Hasse–Minkowski theory is described as resolving Hilbert's eleventh problem.

triage.why: The note asks for a proof that a quinary quadratic form over the field of its coefficients has a nontrivial zero once it is indefinite at the real places. Meyer had proved this over Q in 1884. Hasse's 1923–24 theorem handles general number fields: a form in 5 or more variables always has a zero over every p-adic completion, so the local-global principle leaves only the real places to check. The question is therefore classically settled. It belongs to the circle of Hilbert's 11th problem, but the specific quinary statement is a textbook consequence of Hasse–Minkowski, not a separately published Hilbert problem. Related questions, such as bounds on the size of the smallest solution (Cassels-type bounds), are still studied, but the question as Hilbert stated it is closed.
